Dear Tushar,

I've known you and Ananya since college, so I'm going to say something as your friend, not as anyone's side.
Last Sunday you told me Ananya only nags. On Monday she told me you've stopped caring. I've watched you both for months now, and I don't see either of those things.
What I see is Ananya at the café checking her phone every two minutes, lighting up when it's you. And I see you coming to my place after work just to sit quietly, because going home feels like walking into a test you'll fail.
You're both lonely. Neither of you is the enemy.
I've told Ananya something similar. Talk to her tonight?

Rukmini

You asked how I help friends without meddling, so here's the one I'm proudest of. I'm Leela.
My friend Vasudha and her husband Karan were at war last winter. She kept telling me he'd gone cold. He kept telling his cousin she was impossible to please.
But I'd see her at the office, looking at old photos of them on her phone. And I'd see him at our Sunday lunches, laughing at her jokes a second too late, like he was afraid to join in.
So I told her, gently, "I don't think he's cold. I think he's scared he's failing you." And later I told him, "She isn't trying to nag you. She's lonely."
I didn't pick a side. I just described what I saw.

qa.a: He seemed scared of failing Vasudha, laughing a second too late as if afraid to join in.

I'm Rupali, and Asif and Priti have been my closest friends for years, so I notice things.
At Asif's birthday dinner, Priti sat at the far end of the table. When Asif made a toast, she didn't look up. Later, on the balcony, she told me, "He doesn't need me anymore."
But I'd seen Asif, just before the toast, glance at her seat twice. And when she left the table, he stopped mid-sentence.
I couldn't know what either was feeling for sure. But I said to Priti, "He looked for you twice before the toast." And that night I texted Asif, "She misses you, I think. She's not angry, just lonely."
Neither of them said anything to me after. But they left together, holding hands.

Kamala,

I want to put in writing what we agreed last night, so I can't pretend later that I forgot.
Sunday mornings are ours. Phones off, breakfast on the terrace, no rushing. Every week, not just when things feel bad.

Hemant

The old pattern was: he comes home drained from the hospital, I want to talk, he goes quiet, I push, he goes quieter.
